passage: For this neighborhood exercise, blue calendar squares mean paper collection and green squares mean garden material collection. On Monday, Ana looked at the printed calendar on the noticeboard. A blue square appeared beside Wednesday. The board also displayed a map of the collection route, a telephone number for questions, and a reminder to keep the pavement clear. Ana copied the date into her notebook before walking home. She found a bundle of old newspapers beside a box of dry leaves. The leaves came from the small courtyard behind her building, while the newspapers had been saved in the entrance hall. Her neighbor offered to carry whichever bundle was due first. Ana chose the newspapers for Wednesday because that day's square was blue. She left the leaves for a later garden collection rather than assuming that every kind of material used the same date.

passage: A mosaic border repeats a block containing two red tiles followed by one white tile. Four complete blocks therefore need eight red tiles and four white tiles. A student checks the count by drawing four boxes and placing the three tile marks inside each box. If the design must continue with a fifth complete block, she adds two red tiles and one white tile. The tiles are square and fit tightly along the edge of a cardboard frame. The frame's corners are left undecorated for this exercise, so no special corner pieces enter the calculation. The final count is ten red tiles and five white tiles. Counting only the total of fifteen would hide the separate supply needed for each color. The worked drawing shows both how many blocks are repeated and what each block contains, which makes the color counts easier to explain.
